column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 39: “Allah has pardoned my nation's mistakes and forgetfulness”

column2: From Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Allah has pardoned for me my nation's mistakes and forgetfulness, and what they are coerced into.”
A good (ḥasan) hadith, reported by Ibn Mājah, al-Bayhaqī and others.
Ibn Mājah recorded this hadith by way of al-Awzāʿī, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Ibn Ḥibbān recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ, as did al-Dāraquṭnī, and in their versions it runs: from al-Awzāʿī, from ʿAṭāʾ, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ.
On the face of it this chain is authentic, and all its narrators are relied on as proof in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. Al-Ḥākim recorded it and said: Authentic according to the conditions of both of them.
So he said; but it has a hidden defect. Imam Aḥmad rejected it strongly and said: Nothing is narrated on this except from al-Ḥasan, from the Prophet ﷺ, in mursal form.
Aḥmad was told that al-Walīd ibn Muslim had narrated the like of it from Mālik, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, and he rejected that too.

The hadith of al-Awzāʿī and the hadith of Mālik were mentioned to Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī, and he was told that al-Walīd had also narrated the like of it from Ibn Lahīʿah, from Mūsā ibn Wardān, from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, from the Prophet ﷺ. Abū Ḥātim said:

These are munkar (objectionable) hadiths; they look as though they were fabricated. He also said: Al-Awzāʿī did not hear this hadith from ʿAṭāʾ; he heard it only from a man he did not name — I imagine he is ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir or Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim. And he said: This hadith is not authentic, and its chain is not established.
I say: It has also been narrated from al-Awzāʿī, from ʿAṭāʾ, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, in mursal form, without mention of Ibn ʿAbbās. And Yaḥyā ibn Sulaym narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said:

ʿAṭāʾ said: It has reached me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Allah has pardoned my nation for mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are coerced into.” Al-Jūzajānī recorded it, and this mursal version is the more likely.
It has also come by another route from Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ). Muslim ibn Khālid al-Zanjī narrated it from Saʿīd al-ʿAllāf, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “My nation has been pardoned for three things: mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are coerced into.” Al-Jūzajānī recorded it.
Saʿīd al-ʿAllāf is Saʿīd ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ. Aḥmad said: He is a Makkan. He was asked: What is his standing?
He said: I do not know, and I know of no one who narrated from him except Muslim ibn Khālid. Aḥmad said: This is not marfūʿ; it is only from Ibn ʿAbbās, his own words.
Muhannā transmitted that from him. As for Muslim ibn Khālid, the critics declared him weak.

It has been narrated by a third route, through the narration of Baqiyyah ibn al-Walīd, from ʿAlī al-Hamdānī, from Abū Jamrah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, as marfūʿ; Ḥarb recorded it. Baqiyyah's narrations from his unknown shaykhs are worth nothing.

And it has been narrated by a fourth route, which Ibn ʿAdī recorded by way of ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ibn Zayd al-ʿAmmī, from his father, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ. This ʿAbd al-Raḥīm is weak.
It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by other routes as well. It has already been mentioned that al-Walīd ibn Muslim narrated it from Mālik, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, as marfūʿ.

Al-Ḥākim declared it authentic and called it unusual (gharīb), but according to the most skilled of the hadith masters it is falsely attributed to Mālik, just as Imam Aḥmad and Abū Ḥātim rejected it; both used to say of al-Walīd that he made many mistakes.
Abū ʿUbayd al-Ājurrī transmitted from Abū Dāwūd: Al-Walīd ibn Muslim narrated from Mālik ten hadiths that have no basis, four of them from Nāfiʿ.
I say: It appears that this hadith is among them. And Allah knows best.

Al-Jūzajānī recorded it through the narration of Yazīd ibn Rabīʿah: I heard Abū al-Ashʿath narrate from Thawbān that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has pardoned my nation for three things: mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are coerced into.”
Yazīd ibn Rabīʿah is very weak.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded, through the narration of Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Umm al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has pardoned my nation for three things: mistakes, forgetfulness and coercion.”
Abū Bakr said: I mentioned that to al-Ḥasan, and he said: Yes; do you not recite Qurʾān to that effect: “Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake” [al-Baqarah 2:286]?
Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī is abandoned (matrūk) in hadith.

Ibn Mājah recorded it, but in his version it is from Shahr, from Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, from the Prophet ﷺ: “Allah has pardoned for me my nation's mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are coerced into”; and he did not mention al-Ḥasan's words.
As for the mursal hadith from al-Ḥasan, Hishām ibn Ḥassān narrated it from him, while Manṣūr and ʿAwf narrated it from al-Ḥasan as his own words, without tracing it back to the Prophet ﷺ.
Jaʿfar ibn Jisr ibn Farqad narrated it from his father, from al-Ḥasan, from Abū Bakrah, as marfūʿ; Jaʿfar and his father are both weak.
Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī said: This hadith has no chain that can be relied on as proof. Al-Bayhaqī related this.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When His words, Exalted is He, “Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake,” were revealed, Allah said: I have done so.
And from al-ʿAlāʾ, from his father, from Abū Hurayrah: when it was revealed, He said: Yes. Neither of the two is explicitly marfūʿ.
Al-Dāraquṭnī recorded, through the narration of Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Allah has pardoned my nation for what their souls whisper to them and what they are coerced into, unless they speak of it or act on it.” This is an unusual wording.
Al-Nasāʾī recorded it without mentioning coercion.

Ibn ʿUyaynah narrated it in the same way from Misʿar, from Qatādah, from Zurārah ibn Awfā, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, adding to it: “and what they are coerced into.” Ibn Mājah recorded it.
This addition has been rejected as Ibn ʿUyaynah's; no one corroborated him in it.
The hadith is recorded through the narration of Qatādah in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Sunan and the Musnads without it.

Let us return to explaining the marfūʿ hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās. His words, “Allah has pardoned for me my nation's mistakes and forgetfulness…” to the end, are to be understood as: Allah has lifted mistakes from my nation for my sake, or has let that pass for them; for the verb tajāwaza (“pardoned”) does not take a direct object on its own.
His words: “mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are coerced into.”
As for mistakes and forgetfulness, the Qurʾān has stated explicitly that they are pardoned. Allah the Exalted says:

“Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake” [al-Baqarah 2:286]. And He says: “There is no blame on you for the mistakes you make, but only for what your hearts intend” [al-Aḥzāb 33:5].

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “When a judge gives judgement, exerting himself to find the right answer, and is right, he has two rewards; and when he gives judgement, exerting himself, and is mistaken, he has one reward.”
Al-Ḥasan said: Were it not for what Allah mentioned about these two men — meaning Dāwūd and Sulaymān — I would have thought that the judges were ruined;

for He praised this one for his knowledge and excused that one for his effort of judgement. He meant His words: “And Dāwūd and Sulaymān, when they gave judgement concerning the tillage into which the people's sheep had strayed by night…” [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:78].

As for coercion, the Qurʾān has also stated explicitly that it is pardoned. The Exalted says: “Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief — except one who is coerced while his heart is at rest in faith…” [al-Naḥl 16:106]. And the Exalted says:

“Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers; whoever does that has nothing to do with Allah — unless you guard yourselves against them as a precaution” [Āl ʿImrān 3:28].
We shall discuss this hadith, if Allah wills, in two sections: the first on the ruling on mistakes and forgetfulness, and the second on the ruling on coercion.

Section One: mistakes and forgetfulness. A mistake is when a person intends something by his action, but his action lands on something other than what he intended: for example, he intends to kill a disbeliever, and his killing lands on a Muslim.

Forgetfulness is when a person was aware of something and forgets it at the time of acting. Both are pardoned, in the sense that there is no sin in them; but the lifting of sin does not rule out that some legal ruling may follow from his forgetting.

Thus one who forgets to perform wuḍūʾ and prays thinking he is in a state of purity commits no sin by doing so; yet if it then becomes clear to him that he prayed while in a state of ritual impurity, he must repeat the prayer.
If he forgets to say bismillāh at wuḍūʾ, and we hold that saying it is obligatory, must he repeat the wuḍūʾ?
There are two reported positions of Imam Aḥmad on this.
Likewise, if he forgets to say bismillāh over an animal he slaughters, there are two reported positions from him; most of the jurists hold that it may be eaten.

If he misses a prayer through forgetfulness and then remembers, he must make it up, as he ﷺ said: “Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it but that.” Then he recited: “And establish the prayer for My remembrance” [Ṭā Hā 20:14].
If he prays while carrying some filth that is not excused, and learns of it after his prayer, or during it and removes it, must he repeat his prayer or not?

There are two views on this, which are two reported positions of Aḥmad. It is narrated of the Prophet ﷺ that he took off his sandals during his prayer and completed it, saying: “Jibrīl told me that there was something filthy on them”; and he did not repeat his prayer.

If he speaks during his prayer, forgetting that he is praying, there are two well-known views on whether his prayer is thereby invalidated, and they are two reported positions of Aḥmad. The school of al-Shāfiʿī is that it is not invalidated by that.

If he eats through forgetfulness while fasting, most scholars hold that his fast is not invalidated, acting on his words ﷺ: “Whoever eats or drinks through forgetfulness, let him complete his fast, for it is Allah who fed him and gave him drink.”
Mālik said: He must make it up,

because he is in the position of one who omits the prayer through forgetfulness. The majority say: He has made the intention to fast, and has only committed one of the things it forbids through forgetfulness, so he is pardoned.
If he has intercourse through forgetfulness, is his ruling that of one who eats through forgetfulness or not? There are two views:
The first, which is the well-known position of Aḥmad, is that his fast is invalidated by it and he must make it up; on the expiation there are two reported positions from him.
The second is that his fast is not invalidated by it, as with eating. This is the school of al-Shāfiʿī, and it has been related as a reported position of Aḥmad.
The same disagreement exists over intercourse through forgetfulness while in iḥrām: does it invalidate the rite or not?
If he swears not to do something and then does it, forgetting his oath, or by mistake, thinking it was something other than what he swore about, has he broken his oath or not?
There are three views on this, which are three reported positions of Aḥmad:

The first: he does not break it in any case, even if the oath was by divorce or by manumission. Al-Khallāl rejected this reported position from Aḥmad, saying that it was a slip on the part of whoever transmitted it.
It is the view of al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two views, and of Isḥāq, Abū Thawr and Ibn Abī Shaybah, and it is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ. Isḥāq said: He is to be made to swear that he had forgotten his oath.
The second: he breaks it in every case. This is the view of a number of the Salaf, and of Mālik.

The third: a distinction is made between an oath by divorce or manumission and other oaths. This is the well-known position of Aḥmad and the view of Abū ʿUbayd. Al-Awzāʿī said the same about divorce, saying:

The hadith that has come about pardon for mistakes and forgetfulness applies only for as long as he is forgetful: while he stays with his wife there is no sin on him, but once he remembers he must separate from his wife, for his forgetfulness has gone.
Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī related that the Successors were unanimous that divorce takes effect for one who forgets.
If he kills a believer by mistake, he owes the expiation and the blood money by the text of the Book; and likewise if he destroys someone else's property by mistake, thinking it is his own.

Likewise the majority say of a pilgrim in iḥrām who kills game by mistake, or forgetting that he is in iḥrām, that he owes compensation for it. Some say he owes no compensation unless he killed it deliberately, holding to the apparent sense of His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:
“Whoever of you kills it deliberately, the compensation is the like of what he killed, from livestock…” [al-Māʾidah 5:95]. This is a reported position of Aḥmad.

The majority answered regarding the verse that it attaches both the compensation and Allah's retribution to killing it deliberately, and the two together are specific to one who acts deliberately; when deliberateness is absent the retribution is absent, but the compensation remains established by other evidence.
The most evident view — and Allah knows best — is that the forgetful and the mistaken are pardoned only in the sense that sin is lifted from them,

since sin depends on aims and intentions, and the forgetful and the mistaken have no aim, so there is no sin on them. As for lifting the legal rulings from them, that is not what these texts intend; establishing or negating those rulings needs other evidence.
Section Two: the ruling on one who is coerced. Such a person is of two kinds.

The first is one who has no choice at all and no power to refuse: for example, a man carried by force into a place he has sworn not to enter, or a man carried by force and used to strike someone else until that person dies,

with no power to resist; or a woman held down and then violated without any power to resist. Such a person commits no sin, by agreement, and according to the majority of scholars no breach of oath follows for him.

Disagreement on this has been related from some of the Salaf, such as al-Nakhaʿī, and the like occurs in the words of some of the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad; but the correct view among them is that he does not break his oath in any case.

It is narrated from al-Awzāʿī, concerning a woman who swore about something and whose husband forced her to break her oath, that her expiation falls on him. There is a reported position of Aḥmad to the same effect regarding a man who forces his wife into intercourse while she is fasting or in iḥrām: that her expiation falls on him.
The well-known position from him is that this invalidates her fast and her Ḥajj.
The second kind is one who is coerced by beating or the like until he acts. Legal responsibility attaches to this act, for he could have refrained from doing it, so he chose the act;

but his aim was not the act itself, only warding off harm from himself. He is thus choosing in one respect and not choosing in another, and that is why people have disagreed over whether he is legally responsible or not.

The scholars agree that if he is coerced into killing someone whose life is protected, it is not permissible for him to kill him, for he would be killing him by his own choice, to ransom himself from being killed. This is the consensus of the scholars whose views count;

in the time of Imam Aḥmad, someone whose view does not count disagreed. If he kills him in this situation, the majority hold that both of them, the coercer and the coerced, share in the obligation of retaliation (qawad),
since they share in the killing. This is the view of Mālik, of al-Shāfiʿī in his well-known position, and of Aḥmad. It has also been said that it falls on the coercer alone,

since the coerced has become like a tool. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and one of al-Shāfiʿī's two views. The first view is narrated from Zufar, and it is also narrated from him that it falls on the coerced, because he did the killing directly and is not like a tool,

since he is sinful by agreement. Abū Yūsuf said: There is no retaliation on either of them. Some of the scholars of our school derived this as a view within our school from the reported position under which a group is not executed for killing one person — and this case has an even stronger claim to it.
If he is coerced by beating or the like into destroying property belonging to someone else that is protected, is that permissible for him?

The scholars of our school have two views on this. If we say that it is permissible for him and the owner makes him pay for it, he can claim back what he paid from the coercer. If we say that it is not permissible for him, liability falls on both of them together, as with retaliation.
It has also been said that it falls on the coerced, who did it directly, alone; but this is weak.
If he is coerced into drinking wine or doing some other unlawful act, there are two views on whether coercion makes it permissible:

The first: it is made permissible for him, on the evidence of His words, Exalted is He: “Do not coerce your slave girls into prostitution, if they desire chastity, in order to seek the passing goods of the life of this world; and whoever coerces them — then after their coercion Allah is Forgiving, Merciful” [al-Nūr 24:33]. This was revealed about ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl,

who had two slave girls whom he used to coerce into fornication, though they refused it. This is the view of the majority, such as al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah, and it is the well-known position of Aḥmad. Something similar is narrated from al-Ḥasan, Makḥūl and Masrūq, and there is a report from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that points to it.
Those who hold this view differ over the coercion of a man into fornication. Some say a man can validly be coerced into it and commits no sin; this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī

and of Ibn ʿAqīl among the scholars of our school. Others say a man cannot validly be coerced into it, and bears the sin and the prescribed punishment; this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and Aḥmad's explicit statement, and it is narrated from al-Ḥasan.

The second view: dissimulation (taqiyyah) applies only to words; there is no dissimulation in deeds, and no coercion into them. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and al-Ḍaḥḥāk; it is a reported position of Aḥmad, and it is narrated from Saḥnūn as well.
On this view, if he drinks wine or steals under coercion, he receives the prescribed punishment.
On the first view, if he drinks wine under coercion and then divorces or frees a slave, is his ruling that of one who chose to drink it, or not,
so that his divorce and manumission are void?

The scholars of our school have two views on this. It is narrated from al-Ḥasan, concerning someone who is told, “Prostrate to an idol or we will kill you”: If the idol faces the qiblah, let him prostrate and direct his intention to Allah; if it is in a direction other than the qiblah, he should not do it even if they kill him.

Ibn Ḥabīb the Mālikī said: This is a good view. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: What prevents him from directing his intention to Allah even if it is not towards the qiblah, when the Book of Allah says, “Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:115], and the Sharīʿah permits a traveller to pray voluntary prayers facing other than the qiblah?

As for coercion into words, the scholars agree that it is valid: one who is coerced into saying something unlawful, by coercion that counts as such, may ransom himself by saying it and commits no sin. This is shown by the words of Allah the Exalted: “except one who is coerced while his heart is at rest in faith” [al-Naḥl 16:106].
And the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAmmār: “If they do it again, then do it again.”
The idolaters had tortured him until he would agree with them on the disbelief they wanted from him, and he did so.

As for what is narrated of the Prophet ﷺ, that he counselled a group of his Companions, saying, “Do not associate anything with Allah even if you are cut to pieces and burned,” what is meant is associating partners with Him in the heart,

as the Exalted says: “But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them” [Luqmān 31:15]; and the Exalted says: “but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah” [al-Naḥl 16:106].
Coercion is conceivable for every other kind of speech. If someone is wrongfully coerced into saying anything at all, no legal ruling follows from it,

and it is void; for the words of the coerced came from him while he was not content with them, and that is why he is pardoned and not held to account for them in the rulings of this world or the Hereafter.

In this he differs from the forgetful and the ignorant. It makes no difference whether the words are contracts, such as sale and marriage, or dissolutions, such as khulʿ, divorce and manumission; and the same holds for oaths and vows. This is the view of the majority of scholars: the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad.

Abū Ḥanīfah distinguished between what in his view admits of rescission and carries an option to cancel, such as sale and the like, which he said is not binding under coercion, and what is not of that kind, such as marriage, divorce, manumission and oaths, which he held binding under coercion.
If he swears not to do something and then does it under coercion, he has broken his oath on Abū Ḥanīfah's view. On the view of the majority there are two views:
The first: he does not break it, just as he does not break it when the thing is done to him by force and he cannot resist, as mentioned earlier. This is the view of most of them.
The second: he does break it here,
because he did it by his own choice, unlike the case where he is carried and cannot resist. This is a reported position of Aḥmad and a view of al-Shāfiʿī.

Among al-Shāfiʿī's followers, al-Qaffāl distinguished between an oath by divorce or manumission and other oaths, as we said regarding one who forgets; and some of the scholars of our school derived this as a view within our school.
If he is wrongfully coerced into handing over his wealth, and he sells his real estate in order to hand over its price, is it valid to buy from him or not?
There are two reported positions of Aḥmad on this, and a third reported position from him: if he sells it for its fair price, one may buy from him; if he sells it for less, one may not.

Whenever the coerced person comes to be content with what he was coerced into, because a desire for it has arisen in him after the coercion while the coercion is still in force, then whatever contracts and the like he makes with this intention are valid.
This is the well-known view among the scholars of our school. There is another view that it is not valid either, but that is far-fetched.

As for coercion that is rightful, it does not prevent what one is coerced into from being binding. If a combatant from enemy lands (ḥarbī) is coerced into Islam and accepts it, his Islam is valid; likewise if the judge forces someone to sell his property to pay his debt,

or forces a man who has sworn to abstain from his wife (īlāʾ) to divorce her, once the term of the oath has passed and he has refused to return to her. If someone swore not to pay his debt and the judge compelled him to pay it, he breaks his oath by doing so,
because he actually did what he swore not to do, in a way for which he is not excused.
The scholars of our school mentioned this, as distinct from the case where he refuses to pay and the judge pays on his behalf, in which case he does not break his oath,
because the act he swore about was not done by him.
